title: How the Gym Took Over
tagline: For thousands of years people trained to move. Then, in about a century, we started training to look. This is how it happened, and what got left behind.
intro_markdown:
Walk into any commercial gym today and you'll see the same picture: rows of machines, each built to work one muscle. Mirrors on every wall. Screens counting calories. People training biceps on Monday and legs on Thursday.

It feels like this is just what training *is*. It isn't. It's a recent invention, roughly 150 years old, and it was shaped by showmen, magazine publishers, inventors and marketers as much as by science.

This module traces that story. We start with the Greek gymnasium and old Chinese movement practices, go through the 19th-century gymnastics movements, the strongmen and Muscle Beach, Joe Weider's magazines, Arthur Jones's Nautilus machines and the aerobics boom, and end in today's gym culture, which runs on social media.

One question runs through all of it: **why did the fitness industry end up optimising for looks, for isolated muscles and for whatever a machine can measure, and what did we lose along the way?** The answer to the second half is elasticity, whole-body connection and natural movement. In other words, the qualities that depend on your fascia.

The module ends where this course really begins. In 2007, scientists held the first international congress dedicated to the body's connective-tissue network, and researchers now describe fascia as coming out of "Cinderella-like neglect."

> **Josh's take:** I trained the way the industry told me to. Isolated, machine-based, chasing the look. I got injured over and over and spent a fortune on physio. Understanding *how* we ended up training this way was the first step in understanding why my body kept breaking, and how I fixed it. *(Josh's full story is coming in a dedicated lesson.)*

lessons.title: Before the Gym: When Training Meant Moving
lessons.summary: Long before machines and mirrors, people trained by running, wrestling, throwing, climbing and flowing through whole-body practices. Ancient Greece and ancient China show what training looked like before it was cut into parts.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The original gym had no machines

The word *gym* is ancient Greek. *Gymnasion* comes from *gymnos*, meaning "naked," because men trained there without clothes. They rubbed their bodies with olive oil and scraped it off afterwards with a curved tool called a strigil.

Look at what they actually *did* there. According to the World History Encyclopedia, the typical sports in a Greek gymnasium were wrestling, running, boxing, jumping, discus and gymnastics, many of them accompanied by rhythmic music. Young men also trained for war: archery, javelin and armed combat.

Notice what's missing. No biceps day, no leg-extension machine. Every activity used the whole body as one unit. Wrestling means pushing, pulling, twisting and bracing against a living opponent. Throwing a javelin links your feet to your fingertips in one long chain of force. Running on sand or a dirt track keeps your feet and ankles constantly adapting.

The Greeks also valued things you can't put on a scale. At the annual Hermaia, members of a gymnasium ran a torch race and competed in three categories: *euexia* (vigour), *eutaxia* (discipline) and *philoponia* (endurance). Those are qualities of a whole person, not measurements of a muscle.

## A gym for the body and the mind

Here's the part that matters for this course. The Greek gymnasium wasn't just a place to sweat. Plato's Academy and Aristotle's school at the Lyceum, two of the most famous schools of philosophy in history, grew up at gymnasia in Athens. In Classical Athens, the World History Encyclopedia notes, gymnasia were in effect like modern universities: you trained your body, then listened to lectures and speeches.

The Greeks didn't treat body and mind as separate projects, and that matches the holistic idea behind this whole course: **body, mind and soul are one system.** This course is the body pillar, but it never treats the body in isolation.

To be fair to history, these gymnasia were not open to everyone. A 2nd-century BCE inscription from Beroia restricted attendance to free males up to age 30. Slaves, freedmen and others were barred, and women were excluded too. The ancient world wasn't a fitness utopia. Still, its idea of training was integrated and practical.

## Ancient China: flowing, connected movement

On the other side of the world, a very different tradition grew up. In 1973, archaeologists excavating Tomb 3 at Mawangdui in Hunan Province found a painted silk chart called the *Daoyin Tu*. It comes from a tomb dated to 168 BC and shows 44 figures in standing and sitting postures doing exercises, some of them imitating animals like the bear, monkey, crane and dragon. It's described as the earliest known physical exercise chart in the world.

*Daoyin* (often translated as "guiding and pulling") combined movement, breath and attention. Its exercises included lying, sitting, standing and moving positions. It's considered a precursor of qigong and a formative ingredient in the "soft" martial arts, including tai chi.

Watch tai chi or a good martial artist and you'll see it straight away: slow spirals, long lines of tension from the ground through the hips to the hands, and a body that moves as one connected piece. Many fascia educators describe this kind of movement in terms of continuous connective-tissue lines. Whatever language you use, it isn't isolation. It's integration.

## You were built to move, not to "exercise"

Harvard evolutionary biologist Daniel Lieberman makes a point in his book *Exercised* (2021) that changes how you see the whole story. He argues that humans never evolved to do voluntary exercise for its own sake. For most of human history, people walked, ran, carried, dug and climbed because they had to, and saved energy the rest of the time.

That means "exercise," as a separate activity you schedule, is a modern invention. For most of history, your training *was* your life: carrying water, climbing to gather food, walking long distances over uneven ground. Your body got varied, whole-body, real-world loading every day, without anyone planning it.

This is the baseline. This is the body you inherited: a body designed for varied, springy, whole-body movement, on natural surfaces, in every direction.

## The thread to follow

Keep three words in mind as you go through this module: **whole, varied, elastic.**

- **Whole:** ancient training used the entire body as one unit.
- **Varied:** it covered every direction, surface, speed and type of load.
- **Elastic:** running, jumping, throwing and wrestling all depend on storing and releasing energy, like a spring.

In the lessons ahead you'll watch each of these get chipped away, one invention at a time. By the end you'll see why getting them back is, in Josh's words, *the secret to athleticism.*
key_takeaways: 'Gymnasium' comes from the Greek gymnos (naked); the original gym trained wrestling, running, jumping, throwing, boxing and combat, all whole-body movements.
Greek gymnasia joined body and mind: Plato's Academy and Aristotle's school at the Lyceum grew up at Athenian gymnasia.
The Daoyin Tu silk chart, from a tomb dated to 168 BC, shows 44 figures doing flowing, partly animal-inspired exercises, a forerunner of qigong and tai chi.
Daniel Lieberman argues humans evolved to be active out of necessity, not to 'exercise'; scheduled workouts are a modern invention.
The baseline human body was trained by movement that was whole, varied and elastic.

lessons.title: Physical Culture: Gymnastics, Nations and the Natural Method
lessons.summary: In the 1800s, Europe turned exercise into a system. Jahn built gymnastics apparatus, Ling made exercise a medical science, Zander built the first exercise machines, and Hébert pushed back with a 'natural method.'
lessons.body_markdown:
## When exercise became a system

In the 19th century, industrialisation pulled people out of fields and into factories and offices. For the first time, large numbers of people weren't getting their movement from daily life. Exercise had to be *invented* as a separate activity, and several big personalities rushed to invent it.

Their choices still shape the gym you walk into today.

## Jahn: gymnastics, apparatus and nationalism

In 1811, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn opened the first *Turnplatz*, an open-air gymnasium, at the Hasenheide in Berlin. His *Turnverein* (gymnastics club) movement spread quickly. Admirers called him *Turnvater Jahn*, the "father of gymnastics."

Jahn invented equipment you still know: the **parallel bars, rings, high bar, pommel horse and vaulting horse.** That's a big legacy. Bar and ring work demands serious whole-body strength and control.

But look at *why* he did it. Jahn was a fierce German nationalist who wanted to rebuild his country's physical and moral strength after its humiliation by Napoleon (he also wrote openly hostile things about Poles, the French and Jews). The authorities eventually saw his gymnastics clubs as political, closed the Turnplatz in 1819 and arrested him. Even so, his ideas travelled. In 1825 Charles Beck opened what's described as the first gymnasium in the US, at Round Hill School in Northampton, Massachusetts.

**The shift:** exercise became an organised system with special equipment, built for a political goal.

## Ling: exercise as medicine

In Sweden, Per Henrik Ling (1776-1839) took another route. After daily exercise restored his own health, he studied anatomy and physiology and in 1813 founded the Royal Central Gymnastics Institute in Stockholm. He split gymnastics into four branches: **pedagogical, medical, military and aesthetic.**

Swedish gymnastics was health-focused and anatomy-based. That was a real step forward, but it was also the moment exercise started to be broken into *parts*: specific movements prescribed for specific body regions, like a medical prescription.

## Zander: the first exercise machines

That medical approach led straight to machines. Gustav Zander, a Swedish physician born in Stockholm in 1835 and a follower of Ling's "movement cure," built dozens of exercise devices and founded the Zander Therapeutical Institute in Stockholm. Each machine targeted a specific set of muscles or a specific movement. He is counted among the originators of *mechanotherapy*.

At the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, Zander's machines won a gold medal. By the turn of the century, according to the Smithsonian, they were in health spas across the US, pitched as an answer to a society that now worked in offices without physical exertion.

The US National Park Service, which displays Zander machines at Hot Springs, points out that they used weights and levers to vary resistance and are remarkably similar to the machines in fitness clubs today. A chapter in a Cambridge University Press history volume makes the same connection, arguing that Arthur Jones's Nautilus machines of the 1970s (more on him in Lesson 4) did not come out of nowhere.

**The shift:** for the first time, a machine guides your body along one fixed path. The body becomes a set of separate parts to be worked one at a time.

## Hébert: the rebel who went back to nature

Not everyone liked where this was going. Georges Hébert (1875-1957) was a French naval officer. On 8 May 1902, Mount Pelée erupted on the island of Martinique and destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre. Hébert helped coordinate the escape and rescue of some 700 people.

That experience convinced him that physical training has to be *useful*, and that it has to come with courage and altruism. His motto was **"Être fort pour être utile": be strong to be useful.**

On his voyages Hébert became convinced that the best physical education looked like the movement real life demands: practical, varied, outdoors. He built the *Méthode Naturelle* (Natural Method) around ten fundamental movement groups:

1. Walking
2. Running
3. Jumping
4. Quadrupedal movement (crawling)
5. Climbing
6. Balancing
7. Throwing
8. Lifting
9. Defending (wrestling, boxing)
10. Swimming

Hébert also took on the commercial side of sport. After the 1924 Paris Olympics he publicly condemned sport as corrupted by professionalisation and merchandising, and in 1925 he published *Le sport contre l'éducation physique* ("Sport versus Physical Education"). He was one of the earliest promoters of the *parcours* (obstacle course), and his ideas later influenced parkour and freerunning.

## Two roads split

By 1900, physical culture had split into two paths:

- **The path of parts:** systematised, medicalised, machine-guided, measurable. (Ling, Zander, and eventually the modern gym.)
- **The path of the whole:** natural, varied, useful, whole-body. (Hébert, and before him most of human history.)

Guess which one turned out to be easier to sell.

> **Josh's take:** Hébert's list of ten movements reads like a fascia training plan. Crawling, climbing, throwing, jumping, balancing: every one of them loads the body as a connected system. That's what we're bringing back.
key_takeaways: Industrialisation took movement out of daily life, so exercise had to be invented as a separate activity.
Jahn (1811, Berlin) created organised gymnastics and invented the parallel bars, rings, high bar and pommel horse, all tied to a nationalist goal.
Ling (Stockholm, 1813) made exercise medical and anatomy-based; Zander turned that into some of the first exercise machines, which won gold at Philadelphia in 1876.
Hébert's Méthode Naturelle (motto: 'be strong to be useful') was built on ten natural movement groups and rejected commercialised sport.
By 1900 two paths had formed: training the body in parts (machines, measurement) or as a whole (natural movement).

lessons.title: The Mirror Arrives: Sandow, Macfadden and Muscle Beach
lessons.summary: Around 1900, fitness became a show. Eugen Sandow turned the body into something to look at, Bernarr Macfadden turned it into a media business, and Muscle Beach and Vic Tanny turned it into a lifestyle and then a membership.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The first fitness superstar

Eugen Sandow was born Friedrich Wilhelm Müller in Königsberg, Prussia, in 1867. He made his name as a strongman, winning strongman contests and performing feats of strength on stage. Then he did something that changed fitness for good: he started posing, in what he called "muscle display performances."

Sandow went to museums and measured classical Greek and Roman statues. From those measurements he helped develop "The Grecian Ideal," a formula for the "perfect physique," and he built his own body to match it. That's why he's known as the father of modern bodybuilding.

In 1894, Edison Studios filmed him in a short Kinetoscope film called *Sandow*, now held by the Library of Congress. It shows him flexing, not lifting anything. It's one of the earliest motion pictures ever made, and the body in it is something to **look at**, not something to perform with.

## The first bodybuilding contest

On 14 September 1901, Sandow organised "The Great Competition" at London's Royal Albert Hall, recognised by Guinness World Records as the first modern bodybuilding contest. The judges were Sandow himself, Sherlock Holmes author Sir Arthur Conan Doyle and the sculptor Sir Charles Lawes. Contestants were judged on how their bodies *looked*.

Sandow also ran a magazine (from 1898), wrote books, opened the Sandow Institute (an early gym open to the public), and sold equipment like spring-grip dumbbells. A bronze statue of him, known as "The Sandow," has been presented to every Mr. Olympia winner since 1977.

**The shift:** this is the moment the goal of training moved from *what your body can do* to *how your body looks*. The rest of the industry would build on it.

## Macfadden: fitness becomes media

In America, Bernarr Macfadden (1868-1955) took the idea and built a publishing empire. In 1899 he launched *Physical Culture* magazine. He promoted walking, fasting and natural living, and he railed against white bread, which he called the "staff of death."

Some of his ideas were ahead of their time (walking, wholesome food), some were dangerous (he regarded doctors as quacks), and some were plain eccentric. But his real legacy is the **business model**: health as content, sold through magazines alongside products and personalities. *Physical Culture* became the base of a publishing house that went on to put out *True Story*, *Photoplay* and more.

Sound familiar? It's the ancestor of every fitness influencer you follow.

## Muscle Beach: the golden age, briefly

In the 1930s, on the sand just south of the Santa Monica Pier in California, something special started. The Works Progress Administration, a New Deal agency, installed exercise equipment there, and from 1934 **Muscle Beach** took off.

The original Muscle Beach was mostly about **gymnastics and acrobatics**: people tumbling, balancing, building human pyramids three or four people high and doing hand-balancing in the sun. A weightlifting platform served the bodybuilders. Wikipedia calls it the birthplace of the US physical fitness boom, and the regulars included Jack LaLanne, Vic Tanny and Joe Gold.

Watch the 1948 short film *Muscle Beach* below and look at how those people move: springy, playful, acrobatic, using their whole bodies. For a short while, the look and the movement lived side by side.

It didn't last. The weightlifters and bodybuilders migrated down the coast to Venice Beach, to a weightlifting area known as "The Pen," later renamed Muscle Beach Venice. In 1965 Joe Gold opened a gym in Venice. That gym, **Gold's Gym**, became one of the most famous fitness brands in the world.

## Vic Tanny: the gym becomes a membership

If Sandow made the body a show and Macfadden made it media, Vic Tanny made it a **subscription**.

Tanny and his brother opened a gym near Santa Monica Beach in 1939. After the war, a bigger Santa Monica location became a hub for Muscle Beach regulars. Then Tanny reinvented the gym itself. Earlier gyms had mostly catered to narrow, separate crowds. Tanny's invited everyone, with carpets, bright colours and music, and some later clubs had extras like skating rinks and palm trees behind glass walls. Wikipedia credits him with pioneering the **annual membership**, and his chain grew to some 100 locations across the US and Canada by the early 1960s.

His sales tactics were aggressive enough that the New York State Attorney General imposed a fair-practices code on gyms. Over-expansion eventually bankrupted the chain, and some of its clubs ended up in the Bally Total Fitness network.

## What this era gave and what it took

This era gave us good things: public gyms, the idea that ordinary people can transform their bodies, and some of the most impressive physical specimens in history.

But it also locked in three ideas that still run the industry:

1. **The goal is the look.** Judged by the eye, posed in the mirror.
2. **Fitness is content.** Sold through media and personalities.
3. **The gym is a business.** Built around selling memberships.

None of those three rewards elasticity, coordination or a body that's hard to injure. Those qualities don't photograph well.
key_takeaways: Eugen Sandow built his body to measurements taken from classical statues and helped turn the physique into something to look at.
Sandow's 1901 Royal Albert Hall competition, judged with Arthur Conan Doyle and Charles Lawes, is recognised as the first modern bodybuilding contest.
Bernarr Macfadden's Physical Culture (1899) created the template for fitness as media: content, products and personality.
The original Muscle Beach (Santa Monica, from 1934) was mostly acrobatics and gymnastics before the weightlifters moved to Venice, where Gold's Gym opened in 1965.
Vic Tanny pioneered the commercial gym chain and the annual membership; the gym became a business.

lessons.title: Machines, Magazines and Aerobics: Fitness Becomes an Industry
lessons.summary: From the 1940s to the 1980s, Joe Weider built a bodybuilding media empire, Arthur Jones put isolation machines in every gym, Kenneth Cooper made cardio a number, and Jane Fonda put workouts on VHS. Fitness became a huge industry, built on what could be measured and sold.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Joe Weider: the bodybuilding empire

Joe Weider (1919-2013) published the first issue of his magazine *Your Physique* in 1940, working out of the family home in Montreal. It was renamed *Muscle Builder* in 1953 and *Muscle & Fitness* in 1980. With his brother Ben he co-founded the International Federation of BodyBuilders (IFBB). He created the Mr. Olympia contest (first held in 1965), and his empire grew to include *Flex*, *Men's Fitness*, *Shape* and a line of supplements and equipment.

Weider's most famous protégé was a young Austrian named **Arnold Schwarzenegger**, who credited Weider with inspiring him to take up bodybuilding and come to the United States. The 1977 film *Pumping Iron* made Arnold a household name and pulled bodybuilding into the mainstream. After its release, the number of commercial gyms in the US rose markedly.

Weider's genius was building a **closed loop**: the magazine sold the dream, the contest crowned the heroes, the heroes sold the training system, and the system sold the supplements. It's still the basic business model of fitness today.

And what does a bodybuilding contest reward? Muscle size, definition and symmetry. Things you can *see*. Elasticity, coordination and resilience don't score points on a posing stage.

## Arthur Jones: the machine that isolated the muscle

Arthur Jones (1926-2007) was an inventor with a sharp mind and a strong personality. His big idea: a barbell gives your muscle uneven resistance across a movement, because it's harder at some angles than others. His fix was a specially shaped **cam**, a spiral pulley that varied the resistance through the range of motion. The cam looked like the spiral of a nautilus shell, so he named the machines **Nautilus**. The first one, a pullover machine, was sold in 1970.

Each Nautilus machine was designed to load a specific muscle or movement as completely as possible, with the rest of the body seated, strapped in and stabilised. Jones also promoted **high-intensity training**: short, single sets taken to complete muscular failure.

In May 1973, Jones ran the famous **Colorado Experiment** at Colorado State University, using only Nautilus machines. The headline claim: bodybuilder Casey Viator gained 63 pounds of muscle in 28 days. Look closer and it falls apart. Viator actually gained about 45 pounds of bodyweight, and Jones reached 63 by estimating that he'd also lost 18 pounds of fat. There were only two subjects, and Viator was a former Mr. America regaining muscle he'd had before a two-year layoff. Still, as a story, it became legendary.

Nautilus grew into a huge business, and Jones sold it in 1986 for $23 million. By then, his machines, and the many copies that followed, had changed what a gym looks like.

**The shift:** this is the peak of the path of parts that started with Zander. Machines are clean, safe-looking, easy to teach and easy to measure: plates lifted, reps completed. They train the muscle very well. But they take away almost everything else: balance, ground contact, rotation, whole-body coordination and the springy loading that real-world movement depends on.

## Kenneth Cooper: cardio becomes a number

At the same time, another revolution was going on. Kenneth Cooper, a US Air Force physician, published *Aerobics* in 1968. A summary appeared in *Reader's Digest* that March and spread fast. The book has sold around 30 million copies in 41 languages. When it came out, by Cooper's own recollection, only about 100,000 Americans jogged.

Cooper deserves real credit. He got millions of people moving and changed how medicine thinks about heart health. His system was also built on **points**: you aimed for about 30 to 35 points a week, earned faster the harder you worked.

That was the start of a new habit: turning movement into a **number to hit**. Today it's steps, calories, heart-rate zones and rings to close. Measuring things is useful. But it nudges you to train what's easy to count, like distance, time and calories, and to ignore what isn't, like how springy, coordinated and connected your body feels.

## Jane Fonda and the 80s boom

Then came the VCR. *Jane Fonda's Workout* came out on video in late April 1982. It topped the video sales chart for a total of 41 weeks between 1982 and 1985, boosted VCR sales, and helped open the male-dominated fitness industry to women. "Feel the burn!" became a catchphrase. Fonda sold 17 million videos across the 1982-1995 series.

The 80s fitness boom was real and, in many ways, positive. Millions of people started exercising. Commercial gyms with rows of machines, aerobics studios and big chains became normal parts of everyday life.

## The pattern

Look at what won in this era:

| What got rewarded | What got ignored |
|---|---|
| Muscle size you can see | Elastic recoil you can't |
| Weight on a machine stack | Balance and ground contact |
| Points, minutes, calories | Quality and coordination of movement |
| One muscle at a time | The connections between them |

The industry didn't ignore elasticity and connection because they don't matter. It ignored them because **they were hard to see, hard to measure and hard to sell.**

> **Josh's take:** Machines aren't evil, and neither is bodybuilding. But if they're *all* you do, you're training a body that looks athletic without moving like an athlete. I learned that the hard way.
key_takeaways: Joe Weider built a closed loop of magazine, contest, heroes, training system and supplements; Pumping Iron (1977) took bodybuilding mainstream.
Arthur Jones's Nautilus machines (first sold in 1970) used a spiral cam to load single muscles; they made isolation training the standard in gyms.
The 1973 Colorado Experiment's famous '63 pounds in 28 days' claim rests on two subjects and an estimate, but it became fitness legend.
Kenneth Cooper's Aerobics (1968) got millions moving, and its points system helped start the habit of turning movement into numbers.
Jane Fonda's Workout (1982) and the 80s boom made gyms mainstream; the industry rewarded what was visible, measurable and sellable.

lessons.title: What Got Lost, and the Rediscovery of Fascia
lessons.summary: Today's fitness industry is bigger than ever and runs on mirrors, machines and social media. At the same time, science has rediscovered the tissue the gym forgot: fascia, the connective network that ties your body into one piece.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The biggest it's ever been

The fitness industry has never been bigger. The Health & Fitness Association's 2025 Global Report, covering nearly 30 countries, found that from 2023 to 2024 total membership grew 6%, revenue rose an average of 8%, and the number of facilities grew nearly 4%.

And most of those facilities still look like the gym built in the previous lessons: Zander's and Jones's machines, Sandow's mirror, Tanny's membership model, Weider's supplements, Cooper's numbers.

The new ingredient is the phone. Fitness content is now endless, and it's mostly about how bodies *look*. A 2022 systematic review in *Eating and Weight Disorders* (Jerónimo and Carraça) pulled together 20 studies on "fitspiration" content. In most of them, exposure was linked to more body dissatisfaction, and many also found more appearance comparison and worse mood. The studies were mostly small, involved mostly young women, and were rated low in quality, so the picture isn't complete. But the warning signs are consistent.

Sandow's mirror now fits in your pocket.

## What got lost

Put the whole module together and you can see what a century of training for the look, isolating muscles and chasing numbers left behind:

- **Elasticity.** The spring in your step. Running, jumping, throwing and changing direction all depend on tissue that stores and releases energy. Sitting on a machine doesn't train it.
- **Whole-body connection.** Muscles don't work alone. Force travels from your foot, through your hips and trunk, out to your hands. Machines train the links one by one but rarely the chain.
- **Natural, varied movement.** Hébert's crawling, climbing, balancing and throwing. Muscle Beach's acrobatics. The varied, every-direction loading your ancestors got every day.

All three depend heavily on a tissue that, for most of the 20th century, almost nobody in fitness talked about.

## The forgotten tissue

That tissue is **fascia**: the connective tissue that wraps, links and runs through your muscles, bones and organs as one continuous network.

For a long time, science didn't take it seriously either. The textbook *Fascia in Sport and Movement* (2nd edition, 2021), co-edited by fascia researcher Robert Schleip, puts it bluntly. Fascia, it says, was "literally thrown away in most anatomical dissections" and "treated as a dull and inert packaging organ." Then: "After several decades of a Cinderella-like neglect, fascia has entered the limelight."

Think about what that means. The gym built itself on an anatomy chart of separate muscles, and the tissue that *connects* those muscles was being cut out and thrown away to make the chart.

## The rediscovery: 2007

The turning point is usually dated to **4-5 October 2007**, when the **First International Fascia Research Congress** was held at the Conference Center at Harvard Medical School in Boston. A multidisciplinary committee of scientists and clinicians, including Thomas Findley and Robert Schleip, put it together. It was billed as the first of its kind, and its organisers said it was "intended to be a catalyst" for new research. According to Schleip, all 700 seats were sold out in advance.

The congress has met regularly since: Amsterdam (2009), Vancouver (2012), the Washington, DC area (2015), Berlin (2018), Montreal (2022) and New Orleans (2025). One idea that came out of Schleip's group at Ulm University is especially striking: fascia contains contractile cells called myofibroblasts and may be able to tighten on its own, in a smooth-muscle-like way. In other words, it might not be just passive wrapping.

To be honest about where things stand: fascia research is young and lively, and scientists still argue about plenty of it. Emerging research suggests fascia plays a real role in force transmission, body awareness and even pain. Later modules go through that science in detail.

## Where this course comes in

While the scientists were catching up, coaches and athletes had been exploring fascia training on their own. One of the most influential is **Coach Chong Xie**, author of the book *Secret of Athleticism* and creator of **Hyperarch Fascia Training**. His YouTube channel (@HyperarchFasciaTraining) is the main source this course draws on for fascia theory and practice. His central idea is the **foot-to-glute connection**: a tensioned, responsive foot that links through the fascia of the leg to the glutes and drives explosive movement. In his view it's how well the foot engages that counts, not simply how high your arch is.

That's the core of this course. The gym spent 150 years training your body in parts. **Your body doesn't work in parts.** It works as one connected, elastic system, and you can train it that way, at home, with simple practices.

> **Josh's take:** I'm convinced that when your fascia is healthy, elastic and properly connected, your body becomes extremely hard to injure. That's my lived experience, not a lab result. After years of chronic injuries and expensive physio, I haven't needed a physio since around 2021-2022, and I'm training harder than ever. The rest of this course shows you why I think that is, and how you can do it too.

## Coming up

Module 2 opens up the body: what fascia actually *is*, the major fascial lines, and why the foot-to-glute connection might be the most underrated link in your whole body.
key_takeaways: The fitness industry is at record size (HFA 2025 Global Report: memberships up 6%), but most gyms still follow the isolation, mirror and membership model.
A 2022 systematic review linked 'fitspiration' content to more body dissatisfaction, mostly in young women, though the underlying studies were small and low in quality.
A century of training for the look lost three things: elasticity, whole-body connection and natural, varied movement.
A leading fascia textbook describes the tissue as 'literally thrown away in most anatomical dissections' and emerging from 'Cinderella-like neglect.'
The First International Fascia Research Congress (Harvard Medical School, October 2007) started a wave of research; congresses have met regularly since, most recently in 2025.

lessons.evidence_note: Moderate to strong: the congress dates, textbook quotes and systematic review are well sourced; the industry figures come from a trade association; fascial contractility is a research hypothesis. Chong Xie's foot-to-glute model is a coaching framework without published trial results. The idea that healthy fascia makes injury very unlikely is presented as Josh's lived experience, not established science.
